articles.title: Private care home investors a risk to public sector, regulator says
articles.summary: US investors are buying up UK care homes - a situation regulators say they are "watching carefully" in case it threatens plans for a National Care Service.
articles.body:
Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's ambition to create a universal care service , the regulator says.

The Care Quality Commission's annual report highlights how an increasing share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest have increased their share of the market by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors. Between them they own around one in seven homes.

While there could be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in the quality of care - something the CQC says needs to be monitored.

Meanwhile, home care, providing support to help people wash and dress in their own home, has become more fragmented, with a greater number of smaller providers.

The CQC says this could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people.

In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care.

Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter.

The CQC says the funding system remains fragile – people using care services either self-fund or, for the poorest, the state helps to pay for their costs.

And in some areas, providers are increasingly turning to self-funders, making it more difficult for councils to buy the care they need for those relying on state help.

CQC chief inspector of adult social care, Chris Badger, said the reshaping of the market was happening "largely by accident rather than design", driven by a combination of economic pressure and the problems some councils were having in buying services for those relying on state-funded care.

He said this government's renewed focus on social care – Andy Burnham made it one of his key priorities when he became prime minister – was welcome.

But he said it was important the market was "shaped around what's best for people".

Hugh Alderwick, of the Health Foundation think-tank, said the report by the CQC "lays bare the massive challenges" facing the government.

"The prime minister's commitment to reforming the sector provides an opportunity to fundamentally redraw the state's offer on social care.

"But change is needed now to strengthen the fundamentals of the system.

"Councils need enough funding, the right skills and strong leadership to shape services around people's needs."

Prof Martin Green, of Care England, which represents care providers, said: "If the government and regulators are concerned by consolidation in the care sector, they need to take some clear and tangible action to support smaller care home providers."

He said changes to employer national insurance contributions, inflation and the rising cost of energy was making smaller homes unviable.

"Unless we get some real progress in a funding settlement, the trend of smaller homes closing will be a trend that will continue."

The Department of Health and Social Care said the report demonstrated the "scale of the challenge this government inherited", but said it was committed to overhauling social care.

articles.title: I thought I was dying but it was health anxiety - here's how to recognise the signs
articles.summary: Hollie Sharman shares her experience of health anxiety and a doctor advises on how to manage symptoms.
articles.body:
Hollie Sharman was convinced she was dying. She would go to hospital "four to five times a week" complaining of excruciating chest pain.

"I think the longest I spent in A&E was 13 hours," says the 25-year-old. But despite numerous tests, doctors could never find anything wrong.

Sharman says she had "always worried" about her health as a child and remembers "making up any excuse" to get sent home from school and get into bed.

Her 22nd birthday meal was spent in the restaurant toilets "having the worst panic attack I've ever had".

That triggered years of health anxiety, with hours spent searching symptoms, feeling panicked and isolated.

"I was constantly Googling and using ChatGPT, every source I could get that could tell me what was wrong," she says.

"I spent so long in the hospital. They'd tell me it's nothing, they'd check everything.

"I'd go home, but then my legs would feel weak, so I'd Google that and then it would say it's a sign of heart failure. So I'd go back, it was literally a constant cycle."

At its worst, she "completely disconnected from everyone" and wouldn't reply to messages from family to avoid repetitive conversations.

Sharman says her health anxiety also had an extreme affect on her relationship.

"It got to the point that nothing he said would be the right thing.

"I would get upset because he didn't understand what was going on inside my own head. How can you tell someone everything's fine when I think I'm actually dying?"

Clinical psychologist Dr Kirren Schnack says health anxiety is "a constant worry about being seriously ill or becoming seriously ill when you are not".

Key signs can be "checking" behaviours, such as frequently examining your body, taking your temperature, blood pressure or researching symptoms online.

Another is constantly asking the internet, friends or family for reassurance that you are safe and healthy, she tells Complex with Kimberley Wilson .

Others may experience "avoidance" - not looking at their body or going to doctors appointments because they fear "the worst".

Some may "take on the persona of somebody who has an illness", she adds.

"You may slow down your movements and stop exercising, you're treating yourself and your body and mind as if you are already ill."

Sharman was eventually diagnosed with health anxiety and health-related obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD). She says her family and partner have been "incredibly supportive" and have helped her get to a "better place" with techniques to manage her anxiety.

"I'd write down my symptoms like 'chest pain, excruciating'. And then at the end of the day, I'd write that I was fine.

"And then next time I'd have it, I'd have something to read and I'd be like, but I thought I was dying then and I wasn't."

Sharman says her health anxiety "doesn't control her life any more".

"You need to push yourself and do things when you're anxious, don't put your life on hold because I did for so many years."

Dr Schnack says if you have a symptom that is "new, concerning or doesn't go away", it is "responsible health behaviour" to check the NHS website.

If a symptom has not gone away within two weeks, she advises making a GP appointment. Here's when to call 111, 999 or go to A&E.

And here are some tips from Dr Schnack that might help:

Challenge worst-case thinking - give your brain other explanations for physical sensations; a stiff back might be poor posture rather than a serious illness.

Limit reassurance-seeking - set rules and time limits on how often you ask friends or family about symptoms, and stick to them.

Burn off anxious energy - take quick bursts of movement, like jumping jacks, to help process adrenaline and cortisol.

Ground yourself - use strong sensory experiences such as holding an ice cube or tasting something sour or spicy.

Breathing techniques - take a long breath through your nose, add a second inhale at the top and release it with a long sigh through your mouth.

Ninety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties.

The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks.

With 15 million followers, Droniak has turned her personality into a lucrative business, earning enough from social media to cover her nursing home fees of $12,000 (£9,000) a month.

The Connecticut grandma is one of many older women finding unexpected fame online, with most of their audiences often young enough to be their grandchildren.

From fashion and food to dating and homemaking, they are finding new audiences and, in some cases, a new lease of life.

'I'm showing it's not that bad to get old'

"I always knew I had it in me to be famous, I just didn't think it would happen in my 90s," Droniak tells me, explaining that her grandson began helping her post videos in 2020, initially out of boredom.

She believes her appeal lies in showing younger people that life doesn't stop as you get older.

"They think old people just sit and stare at a wall but I'm showing it's not that bad to get old. We embrace it, can still have fun and I'm still partying and going out sometimes."

Her grandson edits her sponsored content, which includes partnerships with food and beauty brands. As well as paying for her nursing home fees, the money also goes towards a college fund for her great-grandchildren.

Despite being recognised by fans in public, she says her fame feels different at the retirement home. "They don't get it as they don't go on TikTok."

On the other side of the Atlantic, there's Viv Truran, an equally cheeky and cheery 82-year-old from Cardiff.

She started posting on Instagram after losing her husband and her neighbour suggested filming her colourful outfits.

Now she makes two videos a day from her bedroom-turned-studio, showing off her clothes, 22 pairs of glasses and two drawers of scarves.

"I get up in the morning, I never come downstairs until I've done my morning video and I'm very strict about that."

She also keeps a notebook tracking her followers and views – and is now on book five.

Truran is regularly stopped by strangers, many of them women in their 20s and 30s, who tell her they are "frightened of getting old" and she shows them "it's not that bad".

Brands have taken notice too and Truran says she'd "be stupid" not to do deals but is selective.

She does a couple of sponsored posts a month, prioritising local brands and charities like Age UK who paid her several thousand for a recent campaign.

"I've turned down some big deals because it's not my thing. I'm very picky about who I work with, I have to really love the brand."

'I cry when people send me messages from around the world'

Naomi Baker from influencer marketing agency We Are Social says older creators are attractive to brands as they often have "deeply established, highly loyal" communities with greater purchasing power, which "carries a massive premium".

Grace Geramita, 85, has millions of followers who watch her cook recipes she has made for decades.

Known as Nonna Gracie, she moved from Italy to the US when she was 18 and worked multiple jobs at once to provide for her two daughters. Now, she earns more than she ever made in a previous job.

Her grandson Matthew suggested they start filming her cooking six years ago but Geramita wasn't keen as she knew nothing about social media and doesn't "speak very good English", but the videos took off.

"I always cry when people send me messages from all around the world," she says.

Much of her content is about more than food – she says she wants to pass on the "tradition of bringing family together around the table".

Baker from We Are Social says this is part of the appeal of TikTok grannies as they "offer comfort in an uncertain world".

Their wholesome content can also act as a "virtual grandma" for followers, she says.

That's certainly the case for Barbara Costello. The 77-year-old former teacher now shares videos about cooking, cleaning and homemaking skills on her Brunch with Babs accounts.

Her followers tell her she reminds them of their own mothers and grandmothers, with some calling her "the mom I never had".

"Recently, a university student approached me in a restaurant to tell me my cookbook had helped her through her first year living independently and I was so happy."

Costello works with brands but says she has to think carefully about if it's something she wants to put her name on.

She says the best part of being a creator is seeing former pupils at her book signings with their own children.

"It's a full circle moment. I really can't believe this is my life."

articles.title: Magnitude 7 earthquake in Tibet leaves 16 dead, reports say
articles.summary: The quake hit a mountainous, sparsely-populated area in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region.
articles.body:
A magnitude seven earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens of others, according to Chinese state media reports.

The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region as on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.

The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.

Authorities have declared an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 32 others have also been injured.

Power has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, local reports said.

Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.

Strong tremors were also felt in the cities of Qamdo and Nyingchi in Tibet.

Videos on social media show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark, although these have not been independently verified.

The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.

In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.

Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.

Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.

With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

articles.title: Erika Kirk rips 'absurd' 2029 trial timeline for Charlie Kirk's alleged assassin
articles.summary: Erika Kirk is fighting a proposed 2029 trial date for her husband's alleged assassin, calling the defense timeline "grossly out of line" with comparable cases.
articles.body: Erika Kirk is urging a judge to reject a defense proposal that would push the trial of her husband's accused killer into 2029, asking the court to set a trial date in 2027. In a new court filing obtained by Fox News, Kirk's legal team blasted the defense's proposed timeline as "grossly out of line" with comparable cases, asking the court to schedule the trial for the earliest practicable date in 2027. Kirk's team also argued that prolonged delays would deepen the emotional toll on the Kirk family, particularly Charlie Kirk's two young children, and cited a report that Robinson's defense had already cost taxpayers approximately $1.6 million in its first year. "Every additional day of delay carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his two young children who were just three and one year old when their father was murdered and would be seven and five years old by the time a verdict is handed down under the Defense's proposed schedule," the filing reads. JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE Kirk's attorneys cited Utah law guaranteeing crime victims the right to a speedy disposition of charges without unwarranted delay. They also asked the court to require monthly progress reports or status conferences and to consider the family's interests before granting scheduling extensions. Tyler Robinson's defense team proposed a tentative trial start date in the third quarter of 2029, arguing that setting a firm date now would create "false precision" and could jeopardize Robinson's constitutional rights in a death penalty case, where, as the defense noted, "death is different." The defense cited pretrial motions it plans to file through 2029, the volume of evidence still awaiting review and the complexities of jury selection as reasons for the proposed timeline. "From the point of view of defense counsel, appointment to a capital case brings with it a slew of responsibilities that apply in no other context," the defense memorandum states. JUDGE ALLOWS CAMERAS IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION CASE, DELAYS PRELIMINARY HEARING Robinson's attorneys argue that they must review evidence related to both guilt and potential sentencing before trial and that additional evidence is still being processed, making it premature to establish a firm trial date. "It will create unrealistic expectations for the public and the victim's representative, it may cause counsel for both parties to give short shrift to constitutionally required activities, it may rush this Court to deliberate upon and enter rulings on important and complex pretrial motions, and it may jeopardize Mr. Robinson's right to a capital proceeding that has the utmost reliability," the defense states. While prosecutors expect to be ready for trial by Oct. 4, 2027, Utah County Attorney Jeffrey S. Gray argued that beginning the trial in October would mean proceedings would stretch through the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays. TYLER ROBINSON ASKS FOR MORE SECRET HEARINGS AFTER LOSING FIGHT OVER CAMERAS IN COURT "The State therefore proposes that the Court schedule the trial to begin January 31, 2028," the prosecution's memorandum states. Prosecutors estimate the trial would take approximately 17 weeks, while Robinson's defense team anticipates proceedings lasting six to seven months. articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has thrown his support behind a controversial campaign advertisement targeting Democratic candidate Amy Acton in Ohio's closely
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has thrown his support behind a controversial campaign advertisement targeting Democratic candidate Amy Acton in Ohio's closely contested governor's race, urging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to continue running it despite criticism from within his own party.The advertisement features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, challenging her daughter's account of a childhood marked by homelessness and sexual abuse. Arthur also urges voters not to support Acton in the election.Trump endorsed the advertisement in a post on Truth Social on Thursday, while Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a fellow Republican, said the campaign should withdraw it.In his post, Trump did not directly address the allegations of abuse but attacked Acton, writing: "I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!"Family dispute becomes election flashpointActon has said she has not seen her mother since 1978. Her brother, Philip Stearns, has backed her account of being sexually abused by her stepfather during childhood.The stepfather, who died in 2004, had been charged with rape.The advertisement has drawn criticism from Acton's family and campaign, with questions being raised about the use of a deeply personal family dispute in a political contest.As criticism mounted on Tuesday, Ramaswamy's campaign spokesperson Connie Luck issued a statement saying, “We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother ... but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist."Stearns described the advertisement as a “desperate, disgusting attack,” while Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock called Ramaswamy's decision to promote it “both ​despicable and entirely predictable.”Republican governor urges campaign to pull adDeWine criticised the advertisement on Thursday, saying, “It’s just wrong,” and added that he would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take it down.The criticism has put Ramaswamy at odds with a prominent Republican in his own state. Vice President JD Vance, who campaigned alongside Ramaswamy and US Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican, on Wednesday, had brushed aside the backlash.Ramaswamy's campaign has said it is spending $4 million to promote the advertisement.The controversy could also affect the wider Republican campaign in Ohio, where Husted is seeking election to the US Senate against Democrat Sherrod Brown. Polls show Brown ahead in a contest that could help determine which party controls the Senate.Husted said in a statement that he would “not have run that ad".Political fallout could hurt RepublicansDavid Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron, described the advertisement as "campaign malpractice.” He said the controversy could create problems for Republicans beyond the governor's race.Cohen suggested the backlash might alienate some Republican voters, warning, "I think this will either encourage ​some people to switch parties, or more likely, you're going to have a lot of people staying home" on Election Day.Opinion polls show Acton narrowly ahead of Ramaswamy. Analysts have cautioned that an advertisement intended to damage a rival could instead hurt the party behind it, particularly ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tiger Shroff: Attack on Indian actor brings Bollywood's gangster past back into focus
articles.summary: The attack on Shroff has revived memories of the 1990s, when gangsters wielded influence over the industry.
articles.body:
On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor.

Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt .

Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.

Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.

The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi , one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.

Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.

The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.

During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.

Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?

Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.

D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.

In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.

Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke , a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.

Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.

But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad.

"This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."

That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.

Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered . Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.

Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.

Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."

The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.

In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, while Manoj Bajpayee's portrayal of gangster Bhiku Mhatre in Satya became, in the words of film scholar Ashvin Immanuel Devasundaram, "mythologised and talismanic".

The fear and fascination of that era were "seared into the collective consciousness", Devasundaram told the BBC.

Each new attack brings those memories back, he added. But today's gangsters no longer need cinema to build their mythology. Social media allows them to shape their own image, circulating threats, claims of responsibility and carefully staged photographs to audiences far beyond Mumbai.

After the latest shooting, police reportedly stepped up security outside the homes of Khan and Rohit Shetty. The All Indian Cine Workers Association demanded greater protection, asking: "Today it is Tiger Shroff. Who is next?"

There is little evidence so far that criminal networks have regained their former influence over Bollywood's finances and decisions. But the latest attacks have exposed a different vulnerability.

Gangsters may no longer need to control an industry to unsettle it. A single shooting attempt, amplified across millions of phone screens, can spread fear far beyond its intended target.

Sivanandhan, who spent years confronting Mumbai's gangsters, knows the limits of even the tightest security.

"There is always a crack in the armour," he said.

Thoughtful coaching and apparent effort can help you make a better educated professional selection.LibraA professional project might need more intensive scrutiny than normal. Review performance periodically on deadlines, responsibilities and results rather than waiting until the last stage. Frequent checks and fast adjustments may assist keep the project on track and moving toward its planned goals.ScorpioThis is a good time to assess your career goals and think about where you are headed professionally. Go into the debate clear in your mind about what you want, what you have to give and where you are ready to compromise. Pay close attention for clues that might alter the long-term value of the arrangement, not just the short-term rewards. Assuming the talk goes well, don’t jump the gun on commitment before examining the details. articles.title: MrBeast’s $5 billion empire faces scrutiny after media business loses nearly $80 million
articles.summary: MrBeast has turned viral YouTube challenges into something far bigger than online entertainment.
articles.body: MrBeast has turned viral YouTube challenges into something far bigger than online entertainment. Jimmy Donaldson, the creator behind the global sensation, now leads a business empire valued at approximately $5 billion, with interests spanning chocolate, television, theme parks and financial technology. His success shows how a creator can turn millions of loyal viewers into customers. Yet the scale of his ambitions comes with risks. While Feastables has delivered strong sales and major brands compete for his audience, losses in his media business and product controversies raise an important question: can MrBeast build a lasting company that thrives beyond his personal fame?MrBeast’s $5 billion company expands beyond YouTubeDonaldson began uploading videos as a teenager in North Carolina in 2012. His breakthrough came in 2017, when a video showing him counting to 100,000 attracted widespread attention. He later built his channel around expensive challenges, cash prizes and ambitious productions. In June 2026, he became the first individual creator to surpass 500 million YouTube subscribers.That audience has become the foundation of Beast Industries. Rather than relying solely on advertising revenue, Donaldson has used his reach to launch products and secure partnerships with major companies.Feastables, his chocolate brand launched in 2022, is one of the clearest examples. The company generated approximately $250 million in sales and more than $20 million in profit in 2024. Its use of giveaways, familiar branding and retail partnerships helped turn online popularity into purchases.His media ventures have followed a different path. Beast Games, the reality competition launched on Amazon Prime Video in December 2024, offered contestants a $5 million prize. Although the first season became the platform's most-viewed unscripted series, Donaldson said production cost him tens of millions of dollars.Beast Industries' media business reported around $250 million in sales in 2024 but lost nearly $80 million. The company views its content as a way to promote its other ventures, making profitability across the wider business especially important.MrBeast’s business empire faces risks despite major investmentsInvestors have placed substantial value on Donaldson's growing company. A $300 million investment round led by Alpha Wave in 2024 valued Beast Industries at around $5 billion. In January 2026, crypto investment firm Bitmine invested another $200 million.The business has also moved into financial services, acquiring fintech app Step in February 2026. The deal brought access to around seven million users, many of them from Gen Z. Beast Industries has also announced a marketplace connecting creators with major advertisers.However, rapid expansion does not guarantee lasting success. MrBeast Burger faced quality complaints, while his Lunchly food venture drew reports of moldy cheese. He also faced criticism over an AI thumbnail tool, which he removed in June 2025 after creators objected to its similarity to their work.His influence remains a major commercial advantage, but trust can be fragile. Feastables shows that fans may try a product because of its creator, yet quality and value determine whether they return.For MrBeast, the next challenge is clear: turn attention into dependable businesses that can stand on their own. His $5 billion valuation reflects enormous potential, but sustained profits and consumer confidence will ultimately determine whether his empire lasts.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body:
An amber weather warning has come into force in parts of the UK as Storm Austen brings a swathe of powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday.

South West England is forecast to be worst hit by the storm which the Met Office warns could bring travel disruption, power cuts and a possible danger to life.

Wind gusts of 60-70mph, with 80mph in exposed locations, are forecast across Cornwall and parts of Devon, where the Met Office warning is in force until 10:00 BST.

Wind gust of 45-60mph are forecast more widely across most of England and Wales, where two less severe yellow warnings will be in force throughout Friday. A separate yellow warning will also cover part of Scotland, including Glasgow and Edinburgh, from 06:00 BST.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over, bringing a significant risk of transport disruption and there may also be some power cuts.

Winds of this strength will blow some trees over while buildings could also potentially be damaged, leading to a risk of flying debris at the height of the storm.

A number of schools are closed in the impacted areas with many others opening later than usual to avoid the strongest winds.

Train cancellations and speed restrictions are possible because of the increased danger of branches and trees blocking railways.

A number of ferry sailings have also been cancelled, including crossings between Pembrokeshire and Ireland.

Yellow wind warnings cover most of England and Wales with gusts of wind on Friday forecast to reach 45-60mph, with 70mph gusts likely in some places.

As strong as these winds are, the most damaging winds will run to the south of the low pressure centre.

That puts north-west France firmly in the firing line and parts of Brittany could see gusts close to 90mph.

The Channel Islands are also expecting severe gales with gusts up to 80mph.

All schools in Jersey have been told to close on Friday because of the high winds predicted to be caused by Storm Austen.

Heavy rain in Scotland may cause some localised flooding with a Met Office yellow warning for 20-40mm of rain forecast with up to 80mm accumulating in a few areas through Friday.

Storm Boelo to bring travel disruption over the weekend

Closely following Storm Austen will be Storm Boelo, named by the Met Office on Thursday and set to bring another round of stormy weather to the UK over the weekend.

Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the whole of the UK on Saturday with poor travelling conditions expected due to surface water and spray on faster roads and motorways.

The Met Office has issued yellow wind warnings for Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, valid on Saturday and lasting most of Sunday.

Gusts are forecast to reach 50-65mph widely and could reach 80mph in exposed locations.

There could be some localised disruption with strong winds funnelling through the Central Lowlands for a time.

Transport disruption is expected and there may be some power cuts. Following recent spells of wet weather, there is an additional risk of some localised flooding.

Is it unusual to see two storms so close together?

It is not unusual to get storms one after another - in fact they quite often arrive in clusters.

A strong jet stream is needed to rapidly develop powerful wind storms. The process involved in creating such storms involves shifting warmer air northwards and cooler air southwards across vast areas of the Atlantic.

These temperature contrasts can provide a fertile environment for new low pressure systems to develop and if these subsequently get steered beneath a developmental area of a powerful jet stream, they can rapidly develop to create a new named storm with damaging winds.

Although named storms can affect the UK at any time of the year, analysis shows they are much less common in spring and early summer.

May is the only month with no named storms in the 11 years that storms have been named in the UK.

The chances of seeing a storm increases from late summer and throughout autumn with the peak of the season arriving in our winter months.

This increase in storminess is why the storm-naming season begins in September each year.

In about half of the years since 2015, the first storm arrived after 1 November.

articles.title: Clavicular’s Camp Looksmax under scrutiny after teen spends $7,000 and considers $40,000 facial surgery
articles.summary: A Canadian teenager’s secret trip to Los Angeles has drawn attention to the growing influence of looksmaxxing, an online trend that encourages young men
articles.body: A Canadian teenager’s secret trip to Los Angeles has drawn attention to the growing influence of looksmaxxing, an online trend that encourages young men to change their appearance to improve their attractiveness. William Munro, 19, spent $7,000 attending Camp Looksmax, a seven-day retreat led by controversial influencer Clavicular. His parents reportedly panicked when they discovered he had disappeared from home without telling them. Now, Munro is considering facial surgery costing $40,000 after learning about procedures designed to change jaw structure. His experience raises questions about the pressure young men face to meet online beauty standards.William Munro spends $7,000 at Clavicular’s Camp LooksmaxMunro, a business student at Western University in Canada, travelled to Los Angeles without informing his parents. According to USA Today, his family became concerned when they noticed he was missing from his bedroom and contacted him at the airport.Munro initially gave them a limited explanation of looksmaxxing and claimed he had won a YouTuber’s giveaway. He later explained that he had chosen to attend the camp and paid the $7,000 fee with money saved from years of doing odd jobs.“It was a super radical decision,” Munro, who paid $7,000 to go to the camp, told the outlet. “I just thought, I’m a young kid. Money comes and goes. So might as well get the experience out.”Camp Looksmax began its first week on October 1, 2026, with livestreams running around the clock on Clavicular’s Kick channel. The retreat offered participants grooming advice, fashion guidance and tips on approaching women while staying together in a mansion with a private chef.Clavicular, whose real name is reportedly linked to the online looksmaxxing movement, has faced criticism over his conduct and associations. His rape charges were dropped on October 13, according to the report. Munro attended the camp while the charges were still active and said he believed Clavicular’s denial.Looksmaxxing leads to $40,000 facial surgery plansThe camp appears to have influenced Munro’s plans for his appearance. He describes himself as a “decent-looking guy” with a good body but believes he needs to improve his facial aesthetics. He is now considering a $40,000 operation.During the retreat, Munro learned about double jaw surgery, a procedure that can correct jaw alignment problems but may also be pursued for cosmetic reasons. Like other major operations, it carries risks and requires careful medical assessment.Looksmaxxing has gained attention through online communities that promote everything from basic grooming to extreme physical changes. Some practices associated with the movement, including “bonesmashing,” encourage people to strike their jawlines with hammers despite a lack of evidence that the technique works. Such actions can cause serious injuries.Munro said the experience changed how he approaches women, encouraging him to start conversations rather than overthink rejection.“You just got to go out, talk to people, make connections. You know, you see people you think are cool. Just go say anything. Go say hi.”His story highlights the tension between self-improvement and the risks of chasing online ideals. While grooming and confidence can be positive goals, costly surgery deserves independent medical advice and careful consideration, not pressure from internet trends.You use AI every day.
